doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Al Jolson records, old movies and falling for Benny Goodman
summary: His father's Jolson 78 started him; he collected, watched old films and found Goodman's 1938 Carnegie Hall album at the library. He also reflects on minstrelsy and race.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Did you — were you turned on by the Swing Era music, and then the jazz that was being played at the time?

No. It’s all because of my father had a 78, a Decca 78 album of “The Jolson Story” with two pictures of white gloves on the cover. No picture of Jolson or anything like that. And I fell in love with his voice and phrasing. Now I was a strange kid, I mean I’m four years old and this is 1962 and I loved these records. And I used to imitate them, it was kind of strange for a little kid. And that got me into, I mean I was already kind of like — you know I should tie up the Jolson thread just for a moment, that the whole thing about minstrelsy and African-American culture actually wound up getting a head start, my being attracted to Al Jolson and then eventually having to come to terms with minstrelsy in general and Jolson in specific, who’s gotten a very rough deal. He’s become kind of like the straw man for talking about minstrels. It was just very unfair to him. But so unwittingly I was set into something that was going to force me to confront, you know, the overwhelming issue of America and that’s as W.E.B. DuBois put it so many years ago, race. So that pretty much everything I’ve done in my life has been somehow, in some sense been connected with those questions. But I went from there, I was a collector. I used to write NASA and get things about Gemini VI and Gemini, the little home film of the docking and all this kind of stuff. So I was that kind of kid who wanted to write letters and wanted to research things, for whatever, and then, because I wanted to see Al Jolson and then eventually I wanted to see old movies and I wanted to see old Warner Brothers films that were at theaters in New York City like the Theater 80 St. Marks and others, this would be the early 70s, that were showing old movies. And my parents, God Bless them, would bring me in from the suburbs and watch these old movies, which they weren’t particularly interested in. They had seen them when they came out and they weren’t at all interested in nostalgia or anything like that. And then I started seeing Ruby Keeler and Dick Powell and those movies and I kind of loved that stuff. And I was already going buying records and records in the local public library. And then eventually lucked upon Hollywood Hotel, which had Benny Goodman’s band in it. And then all of a

sudden I got this bug about oh boy, well all that other stuff was great but boy there’s something about that that really gets me. Well my local public library had a copy of Benny Goodman’s 1938 Carnegie Hall concert, a double LP, which influenced so many people of a certain age. And I fell in love with it. And I just loved listening to it. And at that point I had been taking — I started piano lessons when I was 4. And you know, a typical thing, an old lady who lived on my little street who had like a living room with heavy drapes — I mean it was your typical whatever that experience was you know. You felt like everyone was looking at you and you sat there and you played in the dark drapes and the old lady and the whole thing. But it worked well, you know what I mean? Not interested in jazz at all or anything like that, but I learned basic the Hanon whatever the heck it was.
